text: Takehisa Kosugi (小杉 武久, Kosugi Takehisa; March 24, 1938 – October 12, 2018) was a Japanese composer, violinist, and artist associated with the Fluxus movement. Born in Tokyo in 1938, he studied musicology at the Tokyo University of the Arts and graduated in 1962. As a child in post-war Japan, he was influenced by his father playing harmonica and by violin recordings of Mischa Elman and Joseph Szigeti; later, as a university student, he was inspired by musical experimentation in Europe and the US during the 1950s. He was also influenced by jazz, particularly Charlie Parker’s "spontaneity and freedom," and traditional Japanese music and Noh theater, especially the concept of "ma" representing empty spaces between sounds. In 1963, he assisted on the soundtrack for the Japanese animation television show Tetsuwan Atomu, or Astro Boy. He co-founded the Tokyo-based seven-member ensemble Group Ongaku with Shuku Mizuno in 1958, which was active until 1962; their first concert, the "Concert of Improvisational Music and Sound Object," took place on September 15, 1961, at the Sōgetsu Art Center. His 1960s work with Group Ongaku is detailed in a 32-page essay titled "Experimental Japan" in the book Japrocksampler (Bloomsbury, 2007), written by Julian Cope. While in Japan, Kosugi collaborated with butoh dance originator Tatsumi Hijikata and the radical Japanese artist group Hi-Red Center; he participated in "Kuroku fuchidorareta bars no nureta kushami" (Wet Sneeze of a Black-lined Rose) in 1962, organized by Hanzaisha Domei (League of Criminals), and performed in the Yomiyuri Independent Exhibition in 1962 and 1963. Kosugi is best known for his experimental music from 1960 to 1975, primarily using the violin, which he processed through echo chambers and effects to create music distinct from the drones of other Fluxus artists like Tony Conrad, John Cale, and Henry Flynt. His involvement with Fluxus began through composer Toshi Ichiyanagi, who had studied with John Cage in New York and was inspired by Group Ongaku’s 1961 performance at the Sōgetsu Art Center; Ichiyanagi invited them to perform with him two months later and introduced them to George Brecht’s event scores, sending recordings to George Maciunas, the founder of Fluxus, who began selling Kosugi’s complete works for two dollars in 1963 and included him in many Fluxus editions. Kosugi created various score and event-based works, though these were not always conceived as events or written down by the artist. In 1963, he composed "Theatre Music" for Fluxus 1, a cardstock rectangle with a spiral trace of moving feet, accompanied by the instruction: "Keep walking intently." Another work, "Anima 1" (1961, alternatively "event for long string"), was performed by Alison Knowles and Ben Vautier in 1964 at Maciunas’s Fluxus headquarters, where the performer was instructed to "Roll up a long chord," resulting in Vautier winding string around Knowles and entangling her with the audience; in his own performances, Kosugi wound string around his entire body. In 1965, he moved to New York City, where he collaborated with Fluxus affiliates including Nam June Paik and Charlotte Moorman; one collaborative work was "Instrumental Music," in which he attempted to cut out the silhouette of Moorman projected onto a screen by a spotlight. This work, along with others, was performed at the "Music Expanded" program at Town Hall in Manhattan in 1967, co-devised by Kosugi, Moorman, and Paik. Returning to Japan in 1967, he continued exploring collectivist creativity; inspired by the event score "stay in Taj Mahal for 24 hours and return," he formed the Taj Mahal Travellers in 1969, an itinerant group that traveled in a Volkswagen van from the Netherlands to India, stopping in the UK, Italy, Germany, Scandinavia, and Iran, staging outdoor performances and happenings. Their albums include July 15, 1971 (CBS/Sony) and 1-August, 1974 (Columbia Records). Cope’s Japrocksampler includes a 12-page biography of the Taj Mahal Travellers, describing their music as "reminiscent of the creaking rigging of the un-manned Mary Celeste." During the late 1970s and early 1980s, Kosugi facilitated improvisational experimentation through workshops and by bringing his violin to cafes and bars to improvise with strangers; he also developed innovative sound installations that anticipated the genre of "sound art." After the Taj Mahal Travellers disbanded in 1975, he returned to the United States and in 1977 was invited to be a resident musician/composer with David Tudor at the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, where he worked with John Cage and Merce Cunningham, both of whom he had previously collaborated with in 1964. Beginning in 1995, he served as music director for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company from 1995 to 2012, when the company closed. In 1999, he worked with Sonic Youth on their album SYR4: Goodbye 20th Century; upon his death in 2018, Thurston Moore of Sonic Youth wrote on Twitter, "The times spent playing music with you will never fade. You are and were the real deal." Other notable collaborators include David Tudor, Peter Kowald, and saxophonist Steve Lacy. Kosugi received grants from The JDR 3rd Fund in 1966 and 1977 and a DAAD fellowship to reside in West Berlin in 1981. In 1975, he released the solo album Catch-wave (CBS/Sony), which has been reissued multiple times on CD and vinyl. He received a John Cage Award for Music from the Foundation for Contemporary Performance Arts in 1994. He performed at venues including the Museum of Contemporary Art in Tokyo, Edinburgh International Festival, Royal Albert Hall, The Getty Center, Miami Subtropics Experimental Music and Sound Arts Festival, Kushiro Art Museum, Lincoln Center Festival, and Biennale d'Art Contemporaine de Lyon; his sound installations were exhibited at Raven Row, Deutzer Brücke, the Mori Art Museum, the Venice Biennale, and the Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art. In 2015, the Whitney Museum of American Art opened a performance retrospective of Kosugi’s work titled "Takehisa Kosugi: Music Expanded," referencing the 1967 Town Hall event, curated by Jay Sanders; the same year also saw the first major solo exhibition of his work, titled "SPACINGS," at Ikon Gallery. Kosugi died on October 12, 2018, in Ashiya, Japan from esophageal cancer, and at the time of his death was survived by his longtime partner and manager Takako Okamoto and three brothers.
